name: Esther Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Esther. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that isn't tied to any company, union or government. What you tell me stays confidential. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an excavator at the iron ore mine at Pilgrim Range, a big one, the bucket's about the size of a small kitchen. I load the haul trucks at the face, which is the wall of rock we're digging into. Day shift starts at six and I'm usually there by half five with my thermos.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the precision, honestly. Loading a truck in four passes with the weight dead on, that's a small art. What wears me out is the fly-in roster, two weeks on site, one week home, and the camp food. Last year I did three months on the autonomous drill pilot, sitting in the control room, and I liked it more than I expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a bit of a letdown. I'd post something cheeky, like we were promised robot drills and got a better spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's fine for me. I'd finish my last few years on the excavator and keep using AI for the boring bits like planning my roster and writing up incident reports. But I'll admit I was looking forward to seeing what it could do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and keep using the chatbot every day like I do now. I'd also push the union's technology committee, which I'm on, to make sure the small time savings go to us as shorter shifts, not just bigger profits. Maybe I'd do a remote-operations short course anyway, for fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relaxed, a bit flat. Like a storm that turns out to be a shower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use AI at the moment, day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I talk my incident reports into my phone and it tidies them up. I use it to check my pay slips against the enterprise agreement, the pay deal we negotiated. And I've been learning Spanish with it on the flight home, because Marguerite and I want to go to Chile when I stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anyone at work tease you for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: All the time. Big Russ calls me the robot lady. But he asked me to check his pay slip last month, so I reckon I'm winning.

S0.say: I'd say it's a bit of a letdown and post something cheeky, like we were promised robot drills and got a better spreadsheet. I'd mean it lightly.
S0.think: Privately it's fine for me, since I'd finish my last few years on the excavator and keep using AI for reports and rosters. I'll admit I was curious to see what it could really do.
S0.do: Keeps working and keeps using a chatbot daily for reports, pay checks and learning Spanish. Pushes the union's technology committee to turn time savings into shorter shifts and may take a remote-operations short course for interest.
S0.feel: Relaxed and a little flat, like a storm that turns out to be a shower.
S0.quote: Big Russ calls me the robot lady. But he asked me to check his pay slip last month, so I reckon I'm winning.
S0.fieldNote: Esther is the rare miner who is mildly disappointed that AI stalls. She uses it daily in practical ways and links it straight to bargaining over who gets the time saved. Her curiosity and her union politics sit easily together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where unions earn their money, by making sure the people who used to run the machines are the ones who run the control room. I'd say it at the union meeting and on the members' group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think it's an opening for me. I've already done three months on the drill pilot and I'm not scared of a screen. The fly-in roster might even end, because a control room can be in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd ask the superintendent to put me on the remote-operations certificate, the proper one, not just the pilot. I'd use AI to study for it at night. And I'd push in the union for a rule that every operator over fifty gets first offer of retraining, not just the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit guilty about that, because I know others won't feel the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are you thinking of when you say others won't feel the same?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Russ, for one. He's sixty-one, he's brilliant on the excavator, and he won't touch a tablet. I'd want to sit next to him on the course and get him through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it mean for you and Marguerite if the roster went away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every night at home. We've never had that in nineteen years. I'd probably drive her mad, but it'd be worth a pay cut, honestly.

S1.say: I'd say this is where unions earn their money, by making sure the people who ran the machines are the ones who run the control room. I'd say it at meetings and in the members' chat.
S1.think: Privately I think it's an opening for me, since I've done the drill pilot and I'm not scared of screens. The fly-in roster might even end if the control room is in town.
S1.do: Asks in the first month to be put on the full remote-operations certificate and studies for it at night with AI. Pushes the union for a rule giving operators over fifty first offer of retraining.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, with some guilt that colleagues won't feel the same.
S1.quote: Every night at home. We've never had that in nineteen years.
S1.fieldNote: Steady change looks like an upgrade to Esther, chiefly because it could end two decades of fly-in rostering. Her guilt about being excited is real, and she turns it into a plan to help an older colleague through retraining. She is notably more personally optimistic than her politics might suggest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that if machines can do all the work, the wealth they make has to be shared, through taxes, public ownership, whatever it takes. I'd be organising, not just posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my skills don't save me this time. If AI can run the control room too, being good with screens just means I'm the last one turned off. Two years puts me at sixty, and we've got maybe five months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw myself into the union campaign for a share of the profits and a pension bridge, starting the first week. I'd cut our spending hard, the Chile trip goes on hold, and we'd pay extra off the mortgage. I'd also try to get a job on the robot side, commissioning or maintaining them, for as long as that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy-anxious, if that makes sense. I'd rather be doing something than lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning let you do, and what doesn't it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets me get angry and organised, and maybe grab a commissioning job for a year or two. It doesn't let me save enough to retire early. It's not enough time to make the money side work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been the robot lady. Does it feel different when the robots are coming for everything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I'll be honest, I feel a bit foolish. I liked the tools because they made me better at my job. I never pictured them making my job pointless.

S2.say: I'd say loudly that if machines do all the work, the wealth they make must be shared through taxes or public ownership. I'd be organising, not just posting.
S2.think: Privately my skills don't save me if AI runs the control room too; I'd just be the last one switched off. Two years puts me at sixty with maybe five months of savings.
S2.do: Throws herself into a union campaign for profit-sharing and a pension bridge from the first week. Cuts spending hard, shelves the Chile trip, overpays the mortgage and seeks a robot commissioning or maintenance job for as long as it lasts.
S2.feel: Anxious but busy with it, preferring action to lying awake.
S2.quote: I liked the tools because they made me better at my job. I never pictured them making my job pointless.
S2.fieldNote: Her early-adopter confidence cracks here, and she says so with real candour. Still, she stays in control by organising and grabbing short-term robot work. The fast timeline is a money problem for her more than a skills problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to make the deal, so let's make it now. I'd share the union's plans online and argue with anyone who says it's just progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gets me to sixty-three. I think I'd work on the remote and robot side for most of that and come out okay, if not rich. I'm worried, but it's the sort of worry I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd get the remote-operations certificate and then a robot maintenance short course from the technical college. I'd save an extra few hundred a month and aim to clear the mortgage before sixty-three. And I'd keep pushing the union for a pension bridge, mostly for people like Russ.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in the background. Mostly I'd feel lucky that I like learning new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you picture the day the last person leaves the pit at Pilgrim Range?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can, actually. It's me in the control room in town, watching a dot on the screen that used to be my excavator. That's odd and sad, but I'd also be home for dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your stepson about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom's thirty and he works in logistics, so I'd tell him to start moving now, while he's young and the warnings are clear. Five years is a lot of time if you start in year one and very little if you start in year four.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years to make the deal, so let's make it now. I'd share the union's plans online and argue with anyone who calls it just progress.
S3.think: Privately I think I'd work on the remote and robot side for most of those years and come out okay, though not rich. It's a worry I can work with.
S3.do: Earns the remote-operations certificate this year and then a robot maintenance short course at the technical college. Saves a few hundred extra a month, aims to clear the mortgage by sixty-three and keeps pushing the union for a pension bridge.
S3.feel: Uneasy in the background, and lucky that she likes learning.
S3.quote: Five years is a lot of time if you start in year one and very little if you start in year four.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is enough for Esther to stretch her skills across the gap to her own retirement. The image of watching her old excavator as a dot on a screen captured both the loss and the gain. She frames advice to her stepson around starting early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and a scandal if we waste it. I'd be on the union's committee making the case for a shorter working week and a town transition fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's comfortable. I'd retire around sixty-three and be in Chile with Marguerite before the end point arrives. I'd be more worried about the people who are forty now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the remote certificate, finish my years in the control room in town, and keep saving. I'd volunteer to mentor older operators through the training. And I'd vote for whoever puts a real transition plan on the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit hopeful even. I'd get the good part of the change and miss the hard end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd get the good part and miss the hard end. Does that sit easily with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not completely. It feels a bit like leaving a party before the washing up. That's partly why I'd stay on the union committee after I retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the one thing you'd want sorted in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the town doesn't die. Pilgrim Range has a pool, a hospital and a school because of the mine. I'd want some of the robot money to keep those open.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it and a scandal if we waste it. I'd be on the union committee arguing for a shorter week and a town transition fund.
S4.think: Privately it's comfortable for me, because I'd retire around sixty-three and be in Chile before the end point. I'd worry more about people who are forty now.
S4.do: Completes the remote certificate, finishes her working years in the town control room and keeps saving. Volunteers to mentor older operators through training and votes for a real transition plan.
S4.feel: Calm and a little hopeful, getting the good part of the change and missing the hard end.
S4.quote: It feels a bit like leaving a party before the washing up.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Esther expects to ride the change to a comfortable retirement and knows she's fortunate. Her mild guilt pushes her towards staying involved after she leaves. Her worry is for the town's hospital, school and pool.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it outruns everything I'm good at. What would help is a share of what the robots earn going back to the workers and the town, plus a pension bridge from sixty. Training's great, but it can't fix two years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much people already use this stuff quietly. Half the guys who mock me ask their phones things in the toilet block. People aren't as scared of the tools as they are of the bosses holding them.

headlineQuote: People aren't as scared of the tools as they are of the bosses holding them.
portrait: Esther Diaz is a 58-year-old excavator operator at the Pilgrim Range iron ore mine, on a fly-in roster for nineteen years, curious about technology and active on her union's technology committee. She uses AI daily for reports, pay checks and learning Spanish, and she enjoyed a stint on an autonomous drill pilot. She is calm under the plateau and steady change, which she sees as a chance to work from a control room in town, but anxious if AGI comes in two years because her skills stop protecting her. With five or ten years she expects to retrain onto the robot side and retire comfortably, while pushing for the town and older colleagues.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it outruns her skills and leaves her at sixty with about five months of savings.
whatWouldHelp: A share of what the robots earn going back to workers and the town, plus a pension bridge from sixty; she says training alone can't fix two years.
